Final expense insurance: shield your family from funeral costs

Final expense insurance is a smaller whole life policy meant to pay for a funeral and last bills, so they do not fall on the people you leave behind. Many policies ask health questions instead of requiring a medical exam, and the premium is usually level for as long as you pay it.

Reviewed by Luay Sadqi, Licensed Agent · NPN 21370662 · Updated November 2026

Schedule an appointment Call (301) 615-8289

What is final expense life insurance?

Final expense insurance, also sold as burial insurance or funeral insurance, is a smaller whole life policy designed for one purpose: to cover the costs that come at the end of life. That means funeral and burial or cremation expenses, plus any final medical bills, lingering credit card balances, or small debts you'd rather not leave behind. Because it's built for these specific costs, the coverage amounts are modest, which keeps the monthly premium lower than a larger policy.

When you pass away, the policy pays a death benefit directly to the beneficiaries you name. The IRS says life insurance proceeds a beneficiary receives because of the insured person's death are generally not taxable income, though any interest paid on them is taxable. Your family can use the money however they need. Many people like the peace of mind of knowing their spouse, children, or whoever they choose won't have to scramble to cover the bill or dip into savings during an already painful time.

Unlike term insurance, a final expense policy is permanent. As long as you pay the premiums, it does not run out at the end of a set term the way term life does.

How qualifying works

A common worry is whether you can qualify, especially after health problems. Here is how it usually works:

  • Health questions instead of an exam on many plans: no needles, no doctor's visit.
  • Options for many health histories, including common conditions like diabetes, high blood pressure and heart conditions. Issue ages vary by insurer.
  • Guaranteed-issue options exist for more serious conditions. They usually have a waiting period before the full benefit applies.
  • Level premiums: on a whole life final expense policy, the premium is usually set when the policy starts and stays level. Check the policy to confirm.
  • Coverage for life, as long as premiums are paid.

Final expense vs. term life — which do you need?

Both are life insurance, but they're built for different jobs. Term life is designed to replace your income during your working years — it pays a large benefit if you die while you're still raising a family or paying off a mortgage, and it expires after a set period like 20 or 30 years. Final expense is permanent and focused on a smaller, specific need: covering end-of-life costs no matter when they come.

The simple difference: Choose term life if you need a large benefit to replace income and protect dependents during your working years. Choose final expense if you want smaller, permanent coverage for funeral and final costs. It does not end after a set term, and the premium is usually level. Many people use term while working, then keep a final expense policy for life. Not sure which fits? See our overview of term and whole life options.

Saw an ad for a government final expense program? Here is what is real. There is no federal final expense insurance program for the public. The ads describe private life insurance that you pay for. State-regulated means your state oversees insurers and agents. It does not mean the state runs or pays for the plan. Social Security has a lump-sum death payment. A spouse might get a one-time payment of $255. If there is no spouse, some children may be eligible. You must apply within 2 years of the death. If you pay for an eligible veteran's burial, VA burial allowances may help. They cover some burial and funeral costs. Check the agent's license. Ask for the name, the agency, and the NPN. Common questions

Final Expense FAQ

Can I qualify with health problems?
Often, yes. Many final expense plans ask a few health questions instead of a medical exam, and some insurers accept common conditions like diabetes and heart disease. Each insurer sets its own rules. If your health is more serious, guaranteed-issue plans skip the health questions, but they have a waiting period. If death happens in the first years of the policy, often the first 2 or 3, the policy may pay only a reduced amount, such as the premiums paid, instead of the full benefit. Graded-benefit plans also pay less in the early years. The exact terms are in the policy, so read them before you buy. See how a graded death benefit works.
Will my premium ever go up?
Usually not. A whole life final expense policy normally sets the premium when the policy starts and keeps it level for as long as you pay it. Check the premium terms in the policy before you buy to confirm yours works that way.
How much coverage do I need?
Many people choose an amount close to the funeral and final bills they expect to leave. We'll help you decide the right amount for your situation without overselling you.
How fast does my family get the money?
The insurer pays after it receives proof of death, such as a certified copy of the death certificate, and the completed claim forms. How long that takes depends on the insurer and the claim. The money goes directly to the beneficiaries you name. Under IRS rules, proceeds paid because of the insured person's death are generally not taxable income, but interest paid on them is.
